analysis.one_liner: Restricts credit card rate hikes, fees, and billing tricks, and shields young adults from prescreened credit offers.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered by the Senate Banking Committee and died there, with no cosponsors and no vote, at the end of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred credit card companies from raising interest rates on existing balances, capped penalty rate increases, limited late and over-limit fees to the actual cost of the violation, and required issuers to check that a borrower can repay before opening an account or raising a credit limit. It would also have stopped sending prescreened credit offers to people under 21 unless they opted in, and required mailed credit offers to state the actual rate and fees. It was introduced in February 2009, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of credit card holders, especially young adults, who would keep their existing interest rate when a card company tries to raise it, avoid fees larger than the issuer's actual cost, and face fewer deceptive 'pre-approved' offers in the mail.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders, especially young adults

how_it_helps.text: Bans retroactive rate increases: if an issuer raises a card's interest rate, the new rate applies only to future borrowing, and existing balances keep the old rate [S3].

Caps any penalty rate increase at 7 percentage points above the prior rate, and allows penalty rates only for specific violations listed in the card contract — not because of a drop in the cardholder's credit score [S3].
Bars late fees and rate hikes if payment is postmarked or electronically initiated by the stated deadline, and limits default fees to amounts reasonably related to the issuer's cost [S3].
Requires issuers to verify, when opening an account or raising a credit limit, that the consumer can make the scheduled payments based on income, obligations, and employment status [S3].

Stops consumer reporting agencies from selling prescreened credit and insurance offers aimed at people under 21 unless the young person opts in, and requires credit offers to disclose the actual APR, fees, and credit limit [S2].
Bars issuers from changing card terms mid-contract, and lets cardholders whose account is closed pay off the balance under the old terms without being forced to repay immediately [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose revenue from retroactive rate increases on existing balances, penalty rates above 7 points, fees beyond their actual costs, and marketing prescreened offers to under-21 consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: The ability-to-pay verification requirement could make it harder for young people, students, and people with low or irregular income to get a first credit card, which many use to build a credit history [S3].
Restricting prescreened offers to adults under 21 would cut off a channel some young consumers use to access credit, unless they affirmatively opt in with a signed notice [S3].

Limits on rates and fees, and the ban on repricing existing balances, would reduce issuer revenue; honest supporters acknowledge issuers could respond by tightening credit availability or raising other prices for borrowers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address practices that repeatedly trapped borrowers in rising debt on balances they had already incurred, and the main cost falls on issuers rather than the public. The clearest trade-off is access: stricter underwriting and limits on marketing to under-21s would protect young people from debt but also make it harder for some of them to get started with credit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on February 6, 2009, with no cosponsors [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill sat in committee for the remainder of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept, for the time being, the ability to raise rates on existing balances, charge penalty rates above 7 points, and collect fees not tied to their actual costs, because no version of these restrictions advanced under this bill.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote was recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no other senator signed on, so the partisan shape of the bill's fate cannot be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have banned raising rates on balances already owed, capped penalty increases at 7 points, limited fees to the issuer's actual cost, and required income verification before issuing cards or raising limits. These provisions target revenue that issuers earn from repricing existing debt and from fees larger than the cost of the event that triggered them.

The bill would bar bureaus from furnishing consumer reports for prescreened credit and insurance offers to anyone under 21 unless that person opts in, and would tighten the definition of a 'firm offer' so mailed offers must state the real rate, fees, and credit limit. Both changes would shrink the prescreened-offer business bureaus sell to lenders and insurers.
